s001.text: UPSC, twenty twenty-two. General Studies Paper Two, ten marks, one hundred and fifty words. Movement and residence are free for citizens, but not absolute. Comment. Here's the strange part. The Constitution itself says so, in one clause.

s002.text: Read what it asks. Comment means give a view, and back it. There are three jobs. Show the right is free, for citizens. Show its limits. Then give a verdict with cases.

s003.text: Start with the right. Article nineteen, one, d and e, gives citizens free movement and residence. Article nineteen says all citizens. So foreigners cannot claim it.

s004.text: But Article nineteen, five, makes it conditional. A law may impose reasonable restrictions. Two grounds are named: the general public interest, and Scheduled Tribe interests.

s005.text: But courts watch the word reasonable. In nineteen fifty-two, Gurbachan Singh upheld externment. In nineteen fifty-four, Ebrahim Vazir Mavat did not allow a citizen's removal. The test is reasonableness.

s006.text: Now we write. One hundred and fifty words, about seven minutes. Open with the right and who holds it. One line.

s007.text: Section one is the limits. Article nineteen five. Article three fifty-eight in an Emergency. And Article sixteen three on residence for some posts.

s008.text: Section two is the cases. Gurbachan Singh. Ebrahim Vazir Mavat. Anuradha Bhasin, in twenty twenty, on section one forty-four. Each has a year and a holding.

s009.text: Close with the verdict. The rights are fundamental yet conditional. A restriction must be by law and reasonable. That is the view the question asks for.

s010.text: Now the easy answer beside it. It says Article nineteen belongs to every person. It says all citizens. It says police can stop anyone at will. It says Gurbachan Singh struck externment down. And it names no case.

s011.text: Here is the payoff. This frame answers its cousins. Twenty seventeen asked about the scope of Fundamental Rights. Twenty twenty-one asked about the Right to Equality. Learn the clause once. The full story gets its own episode in our Polity series.
